title: Vascular Neoplasms
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers tumors and tumor-like lesions built from endothelial cells, from the common benign hemangiomas of infancy to Kaposi sarcoma and angiosarcoma, and adds the primary tumors of the heart. Board questions usually give a patient (an infant, a pregnant woman, a man with AIDS, a transplant recipient, a PVC plant worker) and a lesion, then ask for the cause, the histology, or the likely course. The questions become easy once you can explain why an infantile hemangioma regresses and a cavernous one does not, how HHV-8 genes override p53 and Rb, and why immune status decides how Kaposi sarcoma behaves.

Cell cycle control by cyclin D, CDK4 and CDK6, Rb, E2F, and p53
Properties of benign versus malignant neoplasms and the meaning of clonality
T-cell and NK cell control of virus-infected cells; CD4 depletion in HIV infection
Left atrial and mitral valve anatomy and the diastolic filling sequence

connections.how: HHV-8 and Bartonella produce vascular proliferations, so the organism, not the vessel, is the root cause of two lesions in this chapter.
Loss of T-cell surveillance explains why Kaposi sarcoma spreads in AIDS and after transplantation and shrinks when immunity returns.
A left atrial myxoma obstructs the mitral orifice and can mimic mitral stenosis on examination.
Metastases to the heart are far more common than the primary tumors described here.
Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor, while vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast cause hepatic angiosarcoma.

blocks.text: Benign vascular tumors build well-formed channels lined by a single layer of bland endothelium, whereas malignant ones form irregular channels lined by crowded, atypical cells. A hemangioma is a benign proliferation of endothelial cells, which sets it apart from a vascular malformation, a developmental error in vessel formation whose cells are not proliferating abnormally.
A capillary hemangioma is a well-circumscribed but unencapsulated lobule of closely packed, thin-walled capillaries in skin, subcutaneous tissue, or oral mucosa.

The infantile (juvenile, strawberry) hemangioma is the most common tumor of infancy, affecting about 4 to 5% of infants and occurring more often in girls and in preterm and low birth weight infants. It is absent or only a faint precursor patch at birth, appears in the first weeks of life, and proliferates rapidly for several months. Growth then plateaus, and over years the endothelial cells die by apoptosis and are replaced by fibrofatty tissue, sometimes leaving lax skin or telangiectasias. Superficial lesions are bright red and raised; deep ones are bluish. Lesional endothelium expresses GLUT1 in every phase, a marker otherwise typical of placental capillaries, whereas vascular malformations and congenital hemangiomas (fully formed at birth) are GLUT1 negative.

steps: Absent or faint precursor patch at birth
Appears in the first weeks of life
GLUT1-positive endothelium proliferates rapidly for months
Apoptosis of endothelial cells; fibrofatty replacement
Most have regressed by early childhood
blocks.caption: Regression follows a programmed sequence; location and growth rate decide which lesions cause harm.

blocks.text: Harm comes from where the lesion grows and how fast. Rapid growth can outstrip the blood supply of the overlying skin, so ulceration is the most common complication. A periorbital lesion that blocks the visual axis or compresses the globe causes amblyopia, and a lesion in the beard distribution may involve the subglottic airway. Large segmental facial lesions can be part of PHACE syndrome (posterior fossa malformations, hemangioma, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects such as coarctation, eye anomalies). Large hepatic infantile hemangiomas express type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase, which inactivates thyroid hormone and can cause consumptive hypothyroidism.

A cavernous hemangioma is made of large, dilated, thin-walled channels filled with blood and separated by scant connective tissue. It is less well circumscribed, often extends into deeper tissue, and, because its vessels are mature rather than proliferating, it does not regress. In the liver it is the most common benign tumor, usually a small solitary lesion found incidentally on imaging in adults. Slow flow promotes thrombosis and dystrophic calcification, and needle biopsy risks hemorrhage. One distinction is often tested: the platelet-trapping consumptive coagulopathy of Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon arises in kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma, which are GLUT1 negative, not in the ordinary infantile hemangioma.

blocks.title: Infantile hemangioma, cavernous hemangioma, and port-wine stain
rows: In proportion to the child; darkens and thickens with age
Skin, liver (most common benign liver tumor), brain
Face, often in a trigeminal distribution
PHACE with large segmental facial lesions
blocks.caption: Present at birth and never regresses means malformation; appears after birth, grows, then fades means infantile hemangioma.

blocks.predict: A red facial lesion was fully formed at birth and has grown only in proportion to the child. Would you expect GLUT1 staining and spontaneous regression?
blocks.explain: No to both. A lesion present at birth that grows with the child is a capillary malformation (port-wine stain), not a proliferating tumor, so it is GLUT1 negative and persists.

sections.title: Pyogenic granuloma, cherry hemangioma, and bacillary angiomatosis

blocks.text: Several red vascular papules mimic hemangiomas and Kaposi sarcoma. Telling them apart depends on the patient, the speed of growth, and, above all, the cells that accompany the vessels on histology.

Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is misnamed: it is neither infectious nor granulomatous. It is a rapidly growing, exophytic red polyp, enlarging over weeks, on the skin of the fingers or face or on the gingiva and oral mucosa, often after minor trauma. Histology shows lobules of capillaries divided by fibrous septa within edematous stroma containing inflammatory cells, so it resembles exuberant granulation tissue, and a collar of epidermis often wraps its base. Many small vessels lie under a thin, frequently ulcerated surface, which is why it bleeds with slight contact. The pregnancy tumor (granuloma gravidarum) is a gingival pyogenic granuloma in pregnant women; high estrogen and progesterone amplify the vascular response of the gingiva to local irritants such as dental plaque, and the lesion often regresses after delivery.

Cherry hemangiomas (senile angiomas) are small, bright red, dome-shaped papules on the trunk and proximal limbs. They appear from early adulthood, multiply with age, and are nearly universal in older adults. They are collections of dilated capillaries and venules in the papillary dermis that do not regress and have no malignant potential.

Bacillary angiomatosis is an infection, not a neoplasm. Bartonella henselae (from cats and their fleas) and Bartonella quintana (from the human body louse) are small gram-negative bacilli that, in immunocompromised hosts, especially people with AIDS and very low CD4 counts, induce host cells to produce hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF-1 alpha). This raises VEGF and drives capillary proliferation. The result is red to purple papules and nodules of skin, sometimes with involvement of bone, lymph nodes, or liver (peliosis hepatis, blood-filled hepatic cysts, with B. henselae). Histology shows a capillary proliferation with plump, epithelioid endothelial cells, a neutrophilic infiltrate with nuclear dust, and clumps of granular purple material that a Warthin-Starry silver stain resolves into bacilli. Because living bacteria sustain the proliferation, the lesions disappear when the organism is eradicated.

blocks.caption: Neutrophils and bacteria point to bacillary angiomatosis; spindle cells and slit-like spaces point to Kaposi sarcoma.

blocks.title: A purple papule in a man with AIDS
blocks.text: A man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 40 cells per microliter has several violaceous skin papules, a cat at home, and fever. Both bacillary angiomatosis and Kaposi sarcoma fit the skin finding and the immune state, so the color does not decide. Fever and systemic illness favor an infection. On biopsy, the decision rests on the inflammatory cells and the shape of the vessels: rounded capillaries with plump endothelium, neutrophils, and silver-stain-positive bacilli mean bacillary angiomatosis, whereas fascicles of spindle cells around slit-like spaces with extravasated red cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and nuclear LANA staining mean Kaposi sarcoma. The first resolves when the bacteria are eradicated; the second depends on immune recovery.

sections.title: Kaposi sarcoma pathogenesis and lesion progression

blocks.text: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor of low to intermediate malignancy caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8, Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus), a double-stranded DNA gammaherpesvirus. HHV-8 spreads mainly through saliva and also through sexual contact, transplanted organs, and blood. Infection is necessary but not sufficient: most infected people never develop the tumor, and the usual cofactor is impaired T-cell immunity.

The tumor cell is the spindle cell, an infected cell of endothelial lineage that expresses CD31 and CD34 along with lymphatic endothelial markers such as podoplanin and PROX1. In most spindle cells the virus is latent, kept as a circular episome that expresses only a few genes, and each of them pushes the cell toward division or survival. The viral cyclin, a homolog of cyclin D, binds CDK6, resists the CDK inhibitors p16, p21, and p27, and phosphorylates Rb, freeing E2F to drive the G1 to S transition. LANA tethers the viral episome to host chromosomes so daughter cells inherit it, and it binds and inhibits both p53 and Rb, removing the checkpoint that would arrest or kill a cell with unscheduled proliferation. Viral FLIP activates NF-kappaB and blocks apoptosis.

A small fraction of cells enters lytic replication and secretes viral IL-6 and expresses a constitutively active viral G protein-coupled receptor that increases VEGF. These paracrine signals promote angiogenesis and inflammation, which recruit and stimulate neighboring cells. Early lesions are polyclonal and advanced nodules may become clonal, which is why Kaposi sarcoma has been described as lying between reactive hyperplasia and true neoplasia.

Cytotoxic T cells and NK cells normally hold latently infected cells in check. When HIV depletes CD4 T cells or transplant drugs suppress T-cell activation, infected cells escape and the inflammatory milieu feeds their growth. The fact that lesions often regress when immunity is restored shows that growth still depends partly on an immune-permissive host.

Viral FLIP activates NF-kappaB and blocks apoptosis

Patch progresses to plaque, then nodule
blocks.caption: Latent genes provide proliferation and survival, lytic genes provide paracrine growth signals, and immune suppression removes the brake.

blocks.title: Stages of a Kaposi sarcoma lesion

Irregular dilated vascular spaces with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages; resembles granulation tissue
Dermal spindle cells around jagged channels, extravasated red cells, hemosiderin-laden macrophages
Purple to brown nodule, may ulcerate
Sheets of plump spindle cells with slit-like spaces holding red cells; eosinophilic hyaline globules
blocks.caption: Nuclear staining for LANA identifies HHV-8 in the spindle cells at every stage.

blocks.text: The clinical findings follow from this structure. Slit-like channels leak red cells into tissue, giving the purple color, and hemoglobin breakdown to hemosiderin turns older lesions brown. Involvement of lymphatics and lymph nodes causes lymphedema, and mucosal or visceral lesions bleed. HHV-8 also causes primary effusion lymphoma and multicentric Castleman disease, both more common with HIV infection.

blocks.predict: If a transplant recipient's T-cell immunosuppression were reduced, what would you expect to happen to Kaposi sarcoma lesions, and why?
blocks.explain: They often shrink. Latent HHV-8 genes drive proliferation, but restored cytotoxic T-cell and NK cell activity can again kill infected spindle cells and reduce the inflammatory cytokines that feed them.
blocks.check: The immune control paragraph and the pathogenesis flow.

sections.title: The four clinical forms of Kaposi sarcoma

blocks.text: Every form of Kaposi sarcoma contains HHV-8 and shows the same histology. What differs is the host, and two variables predict how the tumor behaves: how common HHV-8 infection is in the population, and how deeply T-cell immunity is suppressed. Mild immune decline gives slow disease confined to the skin of the legs, while profound suppression gives multifocal disease of skin, mucosa, lymph nodes, and viscera.

blocks.caption: Sites and pace follow immune status: legs and slow in the classic form, everywhere and fast in AIDS.

blocks.text: Classic Kaposi sarcoma occurs where HHV-8 infection is relatively common in the population and where age-related decline in T-cell function is the only cofactor, so lesions grow slowly on the feet and lower legs and patients often die of unrelated causes. Endemic African disease occurs where most people acquire HHV-8 in childhood through saliva. Adults develop nodular or infiltrative limb disease, while children can develop a lymphadenopathic form that progresses quickly even without skin lesions.

Transplant-associated disease arises from reactivation of the recipient's latent virus or from virus carried in the donor organ, in a host whose T cells are pharmacologically suppressed. Because the cofactor is a drug, lesions often regress when immunosuppression is lowered and T-cell control returns.

AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma is the most common form in the United States. It is far more frequent in men who have sex with men than in other groups with HIV, which reflects sexual and salivary transmission of HHV-8 within those networks rather than a property of HIV itself. Lesions appear on the face, trunk, and oral mucosa, especially the hard palate. Gastrointestinal lesions bleed or obstruct, and pulmonary lesions cause dyspnea, hemoptysis, and pleural effusions. Incidence falls when CD4 counts recover, but lesions may flare transiently during early immune reconstitution, when recovering immune cells increase local inflammation.

sections.title: Primary cardiac tumors: atrial myxoma and rhabdomyoma

blocks.text: Primary cardiac tumors are rare, and metastases to the heart are far more common (CV-18-F). Myxoma dominates in adults and rhabdomyoma in children.

Myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, usually appearing in middle age and more often in women. About 90% arise in the atria, with the left atrium affected about four times as often as the right, typically from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis. The tumor ranges from a firm sessile mass to a soft, gelatinous, villous lesion on a stalk. Histologically, stellate or globular myxoma cells, thought to derive from primitive multipotent mesenchymal cells, lie in an abundant acid mucopolysaccharide ground substance, often with hemorrhage and chronic inflammation.

blocks.title: How a pedunculated left atrial myxoma causes symptoms
steps: Stalked mass attached to the atrial septum
Prolapses into the mitral orifice in diastole
Ball-valve obstruction to left ventricular filling
Left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure rise
Dyspnea, pulmonary edema, and positional syncope
Friable fragments break off as systemic emboli
blocks.caption: Obstruction varies with tumor position, so symptoms are episodic and postural.

blocks.text: Three groups of findings follow. Obstruction mimics mitral stenosis, with a diastolic murmur and, as the tumor drops into the ventricle, a low-pitched early diastolic tumor plop; repeated trauma can also damage the leaflets and cause mitral regurgitation. Embolization of friable tumor or overlying thrombus causes stroke or limb ischemia, and a right atrial myxoma embolizes to the lungs. Constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, fatigue, arthralgia) arise because many myxomas secrete IL-6, which drives the hepatic acute phase response, raising ESR and CRP and producing anemia of inflammation. Echocardiography shows a mobile mass attached to the septum. About 10% of myxomas are familial, as part of Carney complex, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in PRKAR1A (a regulatory subunit of protein kinase A); these tumors are often multiple, recur, arise in younger patients and unusual sites, and accompany spotty skin pigmentation and endocrine overactivity.

Rhabdomyoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor of infants and children. It is a hamartoma, often multiple, within the ventricular myocardium, and it is strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis, in which TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) mutation removes inhibition of mTOR and allows excess cell growth. Its large, glycogen-filled myocytes have cytoplasm stretched in strands from a central nucleus to the cell membrane, the so-called spider cells. Rhabdomyomas can obstruct a valve orifice or outflow tract or cause arrhythmias, but many regress spontaneously during early childhood.

blocks.caption: Adult plus left atrium suggests myxoma; child plus multiple ventricular masses suggests rhabdomyoma and tuberous sclerosis.

blocks.title: Syncope that depends on posture
blocks.text: A 45-year-old woman has breathlessness, two fainting spells on standing, low-grade fever, weight loss, and a high ESR. A diastolic sound follows S2, and the murmur changes with position. Fixed mitral stenosis does not change with posture and would not explain fever and weight loss. A mobile mass does both: in some positions a stalked left atrial myxoma falls into the mitral orifice and blocks filling, cardiac output falls, and she faints, while tumor IL-6 drives the acute phase response. The early diastolic sound is a tumor plop, and echocardiography would show the mass on the atrial septum.

Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of endothelial cells. It occurs mainly in older adults and can arise anywhere, most often in the skin (especially of the scalp and face in the elderly), soft tissue, breast, and liver, and it is the most common primary malignant tumor of the heart in adults, usually in the right atrium. Well-differentiated tumors form irregular, anastomosing channels that dissect between collagen bundles and are lined by plump, atypical, multilayered endothelial cells. Poorly differentiated tumors grow as solid sheets of anaplastic spindle or epithelioid cells with mitoses and necrosis, so endothelial markers such as CD31 and ERG are needed to show their lineage.

The classic risk factors fall into two groups. Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to chemical and radiation carcinogens that the liver concentrates or metabolizes. Vinyl chloride, the monomer used to make polyvinyl chloride (PVC) plastic, is oxidized by hepatic cytochrome P450 2E1 to chloroethylene oxide, a reactive epoxide that forms DNA adducts in sinusoidal cells. Arsenic, from pesticides, industrial exposure, or contaminated well water, also causes hepatic angiosarcoma along with skin and lung cancers. Thorotrast, a thorium dioxide contrast agent used from about 1930 to 1950, was taken up by hepatic and splenic macrophages and retained for life, irradiating nearby cells with alpha particles. All three act over long latent periods, often decades.

The second group involves damaged lymphatic drainage and radiation. Chronic lymphedema, classically in the arm after radical mastectomy with axillary node dissection, can give rise to angiosarcoma about a decade later (Stewart-Treves syndrome); impaired local immune surveillance and the growth factor-rich lymphedematous tissue are thought to contribute. Radiation to the breast or chest wall can cause secondary angiosarcoma years later, and these tumors often carry MYC amplification.

Epoxide forms DNA adducts in sinusoidal cells
Mutations accumulate over decades of latency
Malignant endothelial proliferation in the liver
blocks.caption: A metabolic activation step explains why the liver is the target organ.

blocks.title: Angiosarcoma risk factors
rows: Liver; also skin and lung cancers
Arm after radical mastectomy with axillary dissection (Stewart-Treves)
blocks.caption: Hepatic carcinogens act through the liver; lymphedema and radiation act on the damaged field.

blocks.text: Angiosarcoma behaves aggressively. It infiltrates widely beyond its visible margin, is often multifocal in the skin, recurs locally, and metastasizes, frequently to the lungs. Five-year survival is about 30%, and hepatic tumors do worse. Bruise-like purple patches on an elderly scalp, a mass in a chronically swollen arm, or a liver mass in a former PVC worker should all raise this diagnosis.

blocks.predict: Why would a retired PVC worker and a woman with 12 years of arm lymphedema after mastectomy develop the same tumor in different organs?
blocks.explain: Both develop malignant endothelial tumors, but the injury differs. Vinyl chloride is activated in the liver to a DNA-damaging epoxide, so the liver is the target, whereas lymphedema damages the drainage and immune surveillance of one limb, so the tumor arises in that field.
blocks.check: The two groups of risk factors and the table.

integration.text: Each lesion in this chapter is explained by what drives the endothelial cell. Infantile hemangioma has a built-in program of proliferation and apoptosis, pyogenic granuloma is a reactive response to trauma or hormones, bacillary angiomatosis is sustained by bacteria that induce HIF-1 alpha and VEGF, Kaposi sarcoma is driven by viral genes that disable Rb and p53, and angiosarcoma follows DNA damage from chemicals, radiation, or chronic lymphedema. Histology reflects the driver: GLUT1 for the infantile program, neutrophils and bacilli for infection, spindle cells with LANA for HHV-8, and cytologic atypia for true malignancy. Immunology decides the course of the two lesions most tied to AIDS, because both bacillary angiomatosis and Kaposi sarcoma need a host that cannot clear the agent.

The cardiac tumors connect to hemodynamics rather than to vessel biology: a myxoma is benign but dangerous because a mobile mass in the left atrium interrupts filling and sheds emboli, and the systemic symptoms come from a secreted cytokine, not from spread. Genetics links both cardiac tumors to signaling pathways (protein kinase A in Carney complex, mTOR in tuberous sclerosis). Some limits apply: the line between Kaposi sarcoma as hyperplasia and as neoplasm is unsettled, and names such as cavernous hemangioma are reclassified as venous malformations in newer vascular anomaly schemes.

summary: A hemangioma is a benign endothelial neoplasm; a vascular malformation is a developmental error that is present at birth, grows with the child, and never regresses.
Infantile hemangioma appears in the first weeks of life, proliferates for months, then involutes by apoptosis; it is GLUT1 positive, and its harm depends on site (eye, airway, ulceration, PHACE).
Cavernous hemangioma has large mature channels, does not regress, and is the most common benign liver tumor.

Pyogenic granuloma is a bleeding lobular capillary proliferation after trauma or in pregnancy; cherry hemangiomas multiply with age; bacillary angiomatosis is Bartonella infection with neutrophils and silver-stain-positive bacilli.

HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma through latent viral cyclin (Rb phosphorylation), LANA (p53 and Rb inhibition), and viral FLIP (NF-kappaB survival), with lytic viral IL-6 and VEGF as paracrine growth signals.
Kaposi sarcoma progresses from patch to plaque to nodule, with spindle cells around slit-like spaces holding extravasated red cells.

Classic Kaposi sarcoma is slow on the lower legs of older Mediterranean or Eastern European men; endemic disease is aggressive in African children; transplant and AIDS forms are widespread and regress when immunity returns.
Myxoma is the most common adult primary cardiac tumor, usually left atrial, causing ball-valve obstruction, emboli, and IL-6 driven constitutional symptoms.
Rhabdomyoma is the most common pediatric primary cardiac tumor, a hamartoma with spider cells strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis.
Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignant endothelial tumor linked to vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast in the liver and to chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves) and radiation elsewhere.
